items.title: Lions get only 0.001% of the sun's energy that hit their grass
items.claim: Each trophic level passes about 10% of its energy to the next. Sun -> grass -> antelope -> lion. Three steps means lions retain 0.1% of grass energy. Add another step and you're down to 0.01%. The tenth-of-energy rule explains why food chains are short.

options.text: Most of the consumed energy goes to respiration (powering the consumer's metabolism), heat loss, and undigested waste; only a small fraction is converted into new tissue available to the next predator

items.reveal:
Raymond Lindeman (1942) measured energy flow in Cedar Bog Lake, Minnesota. He found progressive losses at each trophic level — formalising 'trophic efficiency'.

Typical values: primary producers fix ~1-2% of incident solar energy as net primary productivity. Herbivores extract ~10% of plant productivity. Carnivores ~10% of herbivore productivity. Top predators get a tiny fraction of the original solar input.

Consequences: food chains rarely exceed 4-5 trophic levels; predators have huge home ranges and small populations; ecosystems with apex predators are inherently fragile to disruption at the base.

The '10% rule' is an approximation. Efficiencies actually vary: ectotherms (fish, reptiles) can transfer 30-40% because they don't spend energy maintaining body heat. Endotherms (mammals, birds) burn most of what they eat to stay warm.

Vegetarian arguments often invoke this: feeding plants directly to people is ~10x more energy-efficient than routing them through livestock first.
items.why: Food chains feel boundless. Thermodynamics caps them at 4 or 5 links. Each predator carries the entropic cost of every prey it ate.

items.title: Plants bend toward light by growing more on the dark side
items.claim: A potted plant on a windowsill tilts toward the window within hours. It doesn't push or twist — it grows ASYMMETRICALLY. Cells on the shaded side elongate faster than cells on the lit side, bending the stem toward the light.

options.text: Auxin (indole-3-acetic acid) accumulates on the shaded side and stimulates cell elongation; this differential auxin distribution was demonstrated by Frits Went and Charles Darwin in classic shoot-tip experiments
Water collects on the dark side
Light evaporates cells on the lit side

items.reveal_title: Darwin's coleoptiles to Went's agar blocks
items.reveal:
Charles Darwin (1880, 'The Power of Movement in Plants', with son Francis) showed that the tip of a grass coleoptile senses light, but the bending occurs lower down — implying a signal travels.

Boysen-Jensen (1913) showed a thin agar block between the tip and the bending region allows the signal through; mica does not. The signal is chemical.

Frits Went (1928) collected the signal in agar blocks and applied it asymmetrically to decapitated coleoptiles, causing bending. The substance was named auxin (Greek auxein, 'to grow').

Mechanism: blue light receptors (phototropins) on the lit side trigger redistribution of PIN auxin efflux carriers. Auxin pumps preferentially to the shaded side. Higher auxin there causes cell wall loosening (expansin proteins) and elongation. The stem bends.

Auxin's reach extends beyond phototropism: apical dominance (shoot tip suppresses lateral buds), root gravitropism (concentrations bend roots DOWN), fruit development, leaf abscission, callus formation in tissue culture. It's the master plant hormone.
items.why: Plant movement seems passive. Phototropism is an active, hormonal, asymmetric growth response — controlled by a single small molecule with effects across the whole plant's life cycle.

items.title: Stomata are tiny mouths that decide between starving and drying
items.claim: A leaf has hundreds of stomata per square millimetre. Open them: CO2 enters for photosynthesis but water evaporates away. Close them: water is saved but photosynthesis stalls. Plants must decide minute by minute.
items.prompt: How do guard cells open and close the stomatal pore?

options.text: Guard cells actively pump K+ ions in; water follows by osmosis; the cell swells; thicker inner walls force the cell to bow outward, opening the pore. Reverse the process to close

items.reveal:
Each stoma is bordered by two guard cells. Their inner walls (facing the pore) are thicker and less elastic than their outer walls.

Opening: blue light activates a proton pump (H+-ATPase). The cells become more negative inside; K+ flows in via channels. Cl- and malate follow. Water enters by osmosis. Turgor rises. The thinner outer walls expand more than the inner walls, pulling the cells apart and opening the pore.

Closing: ABA (abscisic acid, the drought-stress hormone) triggers K+ efflux. The cells lose water and shrink. The pore closes.

Most plants close stomata at night (no photosynthesis needed) and during drought. CAM plants invert this. Wheat loses ~500 kg of water per kg of grain produced — most through stomata.

Climate change is forcing plants to evolve stomatal density: rising CO2 lets leaves get the same carbon with fewer stomata, reducing water loss.
items.why: Stomatal regulation is the central trade-off of land plant life. Engineering stomata for higher water-use efficiency is a major target of crop science.
